enrichment.short_title: Article 8 family life not established for Sri Lankan removal
key_facts: A Sri Lankan asylum seeker appealed against removal after an adjudicator upheld his appeal on Article 8 grounds despite rejecting his asylum claim.
The adjudicator found the appellant had close family in Germany (mother, brother, sister and her family) but no family in Sri Lanka or the United Kingdom.
Contact with the German family consisted of regular telephone calls and a single three-week visit by his sister while he was in the United Kingdom.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal held that family life had to be located in the United Kingdom, but the Court of Appeal rejected that legal test.
On the facts, the court held that the links did not amount to family life within Article 8.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by permission of Schiemann LJ against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision allowing the Secretary of State's appeal from a favourable adjudicator's determination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; removal to Sri Lanka upheld.
enrichment.ratio: There is no absolute rule that Article 8 family life must be located in the United Kingdom, but adult family ties require more than normal emotional affection; telephone contact and a single visit with relatives abroad, without dependency or cohabitation, do not establish family life such that removal would interfere with Article 8 rights.
legal_issues: Whether Article 8 requires family life to be located in the United Kingdom
What factual threshold establishes family life between an adult and relatives abroad
Whether removal to Sri Lanka would disproportionately interfere with family life enjoyed via contact with relatives in Germany
Application of Strasbourg jurisprudence including S v United Kingdom and Abdulaziz

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient sentences increased for child sex offences
key_facts: The Attorney General referred three consolidated cases of unduly lenient sentences for sexual offences against young girls.

TAG was convicted after trial of cruelty, indecent assault and rape of children and friends over many years; his total concurrent sentence of eight years was increased to thirteen years after double jeopardy adjustment.
NJK pleaded guilty to indecent assault and indecency with a child against a seven- or eight-year-old visitor; a community rehabilitation order was replaced with three years' imprisonment.
CCE pleaded guilty to indecent assault on a six-year-old during window fitting work; concurrent six-month sentences were increased to twelve months with extended licence.
All offences were historic, reported late, and caused lasting psychological harm to victims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 following leave to refer three unduly lenient Crown Court sentences; consolidated hearing with reserved reasons.
enrichment.outcome: All three references upheld; substituted increased sentences applying the double jeopardy principle.
enrichment.ratio: In sentencing sexual offences against children, courts must assess harm, culpability and risk using the Millberry dimensions; stale or historic offending does not justify marked leniency where victims kept silence because of threats, shame or the offender's relationship of trust, and different offence types may require consecutive sentences notwithstanding totality.
legal_issues: Application of Millberry sentencing guidelines to non-rape sexual offences
Treatment of historic or stale sexual offending at sentence
Whether cruelty sentences should run consecutively to rape sentences
Availability of extended licence under section 86 for pre-1998 offences
Appropriate custodial length to enable sex offender programme access
linked_authorities: R v Millberry and Others
Attorney General's Reference 39/2002 Peter McKenna
R v Billam

confidence.notes: Three distinct sentencing decisions with detailed facts, substituted terms, and explicit application of Millberry and double jeopardy. Statutory framework for references and licence extension is clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: NASS dispersal quashed for long-resident Jamaican mother
key_facts: A 22-year-old Jamaican woman who had lived in London since age ten applied for indefinite leave to remain and became eligible for National Asylum Support Service support.
She had a Southwark council flat, local friends, a fragile re-established relationship with her mother, a premature baby, and longstanding roots in south London.
NASS refused to pay rent and required dispersal outside London under the asylum seeker dispersal policy.
The Secretary of State treated her three London friends and tentative maternal contact as insufficient to justify an exception.
A psychologist later reported that dispersal would worsen her depression and harm her child.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of NASS decisions requiring dispersal as a condition of support for an asylum/human rights claimant.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; dispersal decisions quashed and remitted for reconsideration; costs awarded; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Although dispersal under section 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 is lawful in general, a decision to disperse a claimant with exceptional roots, support networks and vulnerability in London was irrational and disproportionate, and was likely to breach Article 8 by affecting psychological integrity where dispersal would damage mental health and the child's welfare.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of NASS dispersal policy applied to exceptional long-resident cases
Whether Article 8 private and family life includes psychological integrity
Application of Policy Bulletin No. 31 compassionate exception criteria
Relevance of medical evidence to Article 8 proportionality
Whether NASS must pay rent where dispersal is unlawful
linked_authorities: R (Hetoja) v Secretary of State for the Home Department
Daley

confidence.notes: Collins J's reasoning on exceptional facts, Article 8, and irrationality is detailed. Article 3 merit was not decided. Outcome and quashing order are explicit.

key_facts: Generic manufacturers Teva, Arrow and Generics sought revocation of Merck/Gentili patents for alendronate (EP 2,118,042 and EP 0,998,292).
Patent 042 covering alendronate compositions was held invalid for lack of novelty over Blum and Kabachnik and obvious over Blum, Kabachnik and Fleisch.
Patent 292 claiming weekly 70mg oral dosing for osteoporosis was held invalid as a method of treatment and obvious over Lunar News publications.
The 292 patent's Swiss-form claim was construed as monopolising a dosing regime rather than a new dosage form.
The judge revoked both patents with regret given Merck's commercial investment in alendronate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Patent revocation trial in the Patents Court concerning validity of two alendronate patents challenged by generic drug companies.
enrichment.outcome: Both patents held invalid; revocation ordered.
enrichment.ratio: A pharmaceutical composition or Swiss-form use claim for alendronate was anticipated or obvious from prior art disclosing aminobisphosphonates and structure-activity relationships, and a claim to weekly 70mg dosing for osteoporosis is in substance an unpatentable method of medical treatment following Bristol-Myers Squibb v Baker Norton, being the obvious equivalent of known daily 10mg dosing.

Construction of the skilled person and common general knowledge in bisphosphonate research
Whether weekly 70mg alendronate claims are methods of treatment excluded by section 4(2)
Obviousness of intermittent dosing from Lunar News prior art
Industrial application and Swiss-form claims after Bristol-Myers Squibb v Baker Norton

enrichment.short_title: No binding oral contract to buy PCB invention
key_facts: Mr Wallis invented a method and apparatus for manufacturing double-sided and multi-layer printed circuit boards.
Learonal tested the invention from 1997 and on 16 November 1998 Wallis and Learonal's research director discussed lump sum and royalty terms including £50,000 upfront and 3% of gross worldwide sales.
Wallis claimed a binding oral agreement; Learonal maintained terms were indicative only, subject to technical evaluation, board approval and a formal written contract.
Learonal paid patent attorney fees before an international filing deadline but later declined to proceed after merger with Shipley.
Contemporary correspondence showed no agreement on minimum annual royalties of £30,000 and described negotiations as continuing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Manchester Mercantile Court dismissing Wallis's breach of contract claim; litigant in person appellant.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties discussing a long-term royalty deal for a patented invention left essential terms unresolved, including minimum payments and duration, and subsequent conduct showed continuing negotiation and explicit denial of a firm offer, there was no concluded legally binding oral contract despite handshake and partial performance in funding patent fees.
legal_issues: Whether an oral agreement to purchase invention rights was concluded on all essential terms
Effect of business-agreement presumption to create legal relations where agreement incomplete
Whether payment of patent fees amounted to act in performance of a binding contract
Admissibility and weight of post-meeting correspondence on intention to contract
Whether further technical testing precluded immediate binding agreement

enrichment.short_title: Crown Court could not dismiss appeal for non-attendance
key_facts: Sean Hayes appealed to Chelmsford Crown Court against magistrates' convictions for theft and related offences.
He was granted bail pending appeal but repeatedly failed to attend appeal hearings without explanation or medical evidence.
On 9 May 2002, represented by counsel but absent in person, HHJ Ball QC dismissed the appeal for want of prosecution and awarded costs.
The appellant's counsel did not apply to abandon the appeal and did not consent to dismissal.
The case was stated for the Divisional Court on whether persistent non-attendance could amount to de facto abandonment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Crown Court dismissal of a conviction appeal where the appellant on bail failed to attend but was represented by counsel.
enrichment.outcome: Question answered in the negative; Crown Court decision and costs order quashed; Crown Court directed to hear the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where an appellant is represented on a Crown Court conviction appeal he is deemed present under section 112 of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980, and the court has no power to dismiss the appeal without hearing evidence simply because a bailed appellant persistently fails to attend; the proper course is to hear the appeal in his absence under ex parte Clair, Brewer and Podmore.
legal_issues: Whether persistent failure to attend a bailed appeal amounts to de facto abandonment
Effect of representation deeming an absent appellant present under section 112
Distinction between appellants on bail with a duty to attend and those not so obliged
Whether Crown Court may dismiss an appeal without hearing evidence
Application of rule 11 Crown Court Rules 1982 on abandonment

enrichment.short_title: Farm track access and shooting-rights development upheld
key_facts: Well Barn Estate reserved sporting rights and a brown-track vehicular right of way over Warren Farm when Shackleton bought the freehold in 1991.
The estate installed a 24-foot gate at the top of the track to access adjoining blue land; the Shackletons disputed agricultural access beyond the brown-coloured track.

The judge implied a right of access at Point A and granted negative declarations that barn conversion development would not substantially interfere with shooting rights, subject to covenants and undertakings.
Shackleton obtained planning permission to convert farm buildings to residential use after failed £800,000 purchase negotiations.
The estate's shoot relied on beaters crossing Warren Farm during partridge drives.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Oxford County Court/Chancery transfer concerning declaratory relief on right of way and counterclaim declarations on residential development despite reserved sporting rights.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; declarations and covenants upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A right of way reserved over a brown-coloured track implied reasonable agricultural access at its natural end, and where joint-names insurance and no-recourse covenants allocate fire risk to the employer, a negative declaration may properly confirm that permitted residential development will not substantially interfere with reserved sporting rights if bounded by height limits, construction timing and use restrictions.
legal_issues: Construction of a reserved vehicular right of way over a farm track and verges
Implied access from track to retained land and reasonable gate width
Rectification for unilateral mistake as to plan colouring

Appropriateness of negative declarations with undertakings in property disputes

enrichment.short_title: Contractor not liable for negligently caused pub fire
key_facts: GD Construction refurbished The Thatchers public house in Reading under JCT IFC 84 with clause 6.3C applying to existing structures at the employer's sole insurance risk.
The employer failed to take out the required joint-names insurance against specified perils including fire.
A roofer's negligent use of a blow torch ignited the thatched roof in November 1996, causing extensive damage to the existing structure.
The employer sued for repair costs of about £436,000; the contractor argued liability was excluded because fire damage to existing structures was a specified peril the employer should have insured.
The preliminary issue assumed negligence by the contractor's subcontractor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Technology and Construction Court preliminary issue on contractor liability for fire damage to existing structures under IFC 84 clauses 6.1.2 and 6.3C.1.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; preliminary issue answered in the negative as to liability for existing-structure repair costs.
enrichment.ratio: Under IFC 84 where clause 6.3C.1 requires the employer to insure existing structures in joint names against specified perils including fire, the exclusion in clause 6.1.2 removes the contractor's negligence-based liability for fire damage to that insured property, because fire in an insurance context covers negligently caused fire and the contractual scheme allocates that risk to the employer's joint-names policy.
legal_issues: Construction of clause 6.1.2 liability and indemnity alongside clause 6.3C.1 insurance obligations
Whether specified peril fire includes negligently caused fire
Effect of employer's failure to obtain required joint-names insurance
Application of Archdale, Scottish Special Housing and Co-operative Retail Services v Taylor Young
Distinction from Dorset CC and Barking cases lacking express exclusion linkage

enrichment.short_title: ACT compensation unaffected by Article 10 DTA payments
key_facts: Pirelli UK and Pirelli General paid advance corporation tax on dividends to Italian and Netherlands parent companies between 1995 and 1999.
United Kingdom law denied section 247 group income elections to non-UK parents, contrary to Metallgesellschaft/Hoechst.
Italian and Netherlands double taxation agreements entitled the foreign parents to Article 10 DTA payments equal to 6.875% of dividends received.
The Revenue argued those DTA payments countervailed ACT compensation owed to the UK subsidiaries.
Park J held the DTA payments would still have been payable even if dividends had been paid as group income without ACT.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Group litigation test case in the Chancery Division on Pirelli claims for ACT compensation following Metallgesellschaft/Hoechst.
enrichment.outcome: Pirelli claimants succeeded on the Article 52/43 issue; Athinaiki Parent and Subsidiary Directive issue deferred for possible CJEC reference.
enrichment.ratio: Receipt by foreign parent companies of Article 10 double taxation agreement payments does not reduce compensation or restitution payable to United Kingdom subsidiaries for ACT unlawfully paid, because those DTA payments would have remained payable even if section 247 elections had permitted group income dividends without ACT, and the breach of Community law was suffered at subsidiary level not group level.
legal_issues: Whether Article 10 DTA payments offset Metallgesellschaft ACT restitution claims
Construction of Italian and Netherlands DTAs conferring tax credits on corporate shareholders
Whether parent and subsidiary should be treated as a single person for tax compensation
Scope of Metallgesellschaft/Hoechst compensation at subsidiary versus group level
Whether ACT is a withholding tax under the Parent and Subsidiary Directive after Athinaiki

enrichment.short_title: Prisoner judicial reviews given procedural directions
key_facts: Mr Dhanota, a serving prisoner and prolific litigant, had five related judicial review applications concerning prison conditions and procedures.
Gibbs J had previously dismissed eight appeals and described the applicant's conduct as vexatious.
Applications covered IT access, PIN telephones, handcuffing at court, private cash limits, and the prison canteen system.
Newman J declined to treat the directions hearing as an oral permission hearing and preserved the applicant's right to renewal before a single judge.
Concessions were made on IT compact terms, printing facilities, and access to legal CDs once delivered to the prison.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Directions hearing in five consolidated prisoner judicial review claims raising Convention-based challenges; not a final disposal on merits.
enrichment.outcome: Procedural directions only; several claims to be reconsidered, withdrawn or joined with related prisoner cases; no final relief granted on merits.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a prisoner litigant's history suggests vexatious conduct, a directions judge should not convert a case-management hearing into a final oral permission hearing without preserving procedural rights to paper determination and renewal, while individual claims lacking Article 8(2) analysis, adequate grounds, or raising abuse of process may properly be directed toward withdrawal.
legal_issues: Prisoners' Article 6 right of access to court and IT facilities
Lawfulness of PIN telephone systems and data protection concerns
Handcuffing applications at court and security file practice
Private cash limits and funding of legal proceedings from prison accounts
Whether repeated handcuffing and canteen claims constitute abuse of process
linked_authorities: R v Mullen

confidence.notes: Judgment is primarily procedural with partial concessions and directions rather than final merits decisions. Convention articles are invoked by the claimant but several claims were flagged as weak or abusive; ratio focuses on procedure and case management.
